query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Under high-temperature sliding conditions, the overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation behavior of a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating are governed by a dynamic, shear-induced transformation of the near-surface microstructure. Specifically, sliding promotes localized deformation that refines the as-deposited coarse microstructure into an ultra‐nanocrystalline, twinned tribolayer which homogenizes stress distribution and retards further dislocation slip, thereby decreasing wear and minimizing severe localized deformation.
generation.material_initial_state: A FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating deposited on a conventional metal substrate with a relatively coarse grain microstructure (as-deposited state) without any post-treatment to induce nanocrystallinity.
generation.intervention: Apply a rapid post-deposition thermal annealing treatment designed to pre-induce nanocrystalline grain refinement and an increased density of deformation twins in the coating.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests conducted at elevated temperatures (approximately 500 °C) in an inert or controlled atmosphere to minimize oxidation effects.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline tribolayer enriched in deformation twins and high dislocation density at the coating surface.
generation.mechanism: Shear-induced dynamic recrystallization during sliding—augmented by pre-existing nanocrystallinity from thermal annealing—leads to a transformation of the coarse microstructure into a finely twinned tribolayer. This refined layer redistributes local stresses more uniformly, impedes crack initiation, and reduces localized deformation, thereby enhancing wear resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: The annealed coating is expected to exhibit lower wear rates and a reduction in stress drop events during sliding, compared to the baseline untreated coating, due to the improved load distribution and resistance to microcrack initiation.
generation.baseline: The as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating without any additional thermal treatment, exhibiting a relatively coarse microstructure.
generation.boundary: These predictions are most applicable under high-temperature sliding conditions (~500 °C) in an environment that minimizes oxidation; in regimes where oxidation or other surface reactions dominate, the mechanism might be altered.
generation.uncertainty: The exact degree of grain refinement and twin density necessary for optimum wear performance is not fully quantified, and the interplay with potential high-temperature oxidation remains to be clarified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical FeNiCrCoCu coatings on conventional metal substrates: one set receives the rapid post-deposition thermal annealing treatment to induce nanocrystalline refinement and twin formation, while the other set is retained in the as-deposited state. Conduct controlled high-temperature sliding wear tests (at ~500 °C in an inert atmosphere) on both sets. After testing, examine the worn surfaces using SEM/TEM to quantify grain size, twin density, and microstructural evolution; record wear volume loss and friction coefficient.
measurements: Surface and cross-sectional microstructural analysis (grain size, twin density, dislocation density) via SEM/TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermally annealed coatings do not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in wear volume and smoother, more homogeneous deformation (i.e., a clearly refined, twinned tribolayer is absent) relative to the as-deposited coatings, then the hypothesis—that shear-induced nanocrystallization and twin formation govern the enhanced wear resistance—would be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractAl1.8CrCuFeNi2 high-entropy alloy coatings with different TiC contents were prepared using laser cladding. The effect of TiC on the microstructure, hardness and wear resistance of the coatings was investigated. It was found that the phase structure of the coating with 10 wt.% TiC was a single BCC phase with no other precipitated phase. When 20 wt.% TiC was added, the phase structure of the coating was a BCC phase and TiC phase. When the TiC content increased to 30 wt.%, more TiC-reinforcing phase was formed. With the increase in the TiC content, the hardness of the high-entropy alloy coating was enhanced and the wear loss clearly decreased, which was closely related to the change in the coating structure. The addition of TiC to high-entropy alloys plays the role of fine-grain strengthening and dispersion strengthening.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, wear resistance, coatings, titanium carbide
